question.:question/worked-solution:
$$
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
$$

Let $u=2\coth x+1$. Differentiating gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=-2\csch^2 x,
\qquad \csch^2 x\,\mathrm{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u.$$

Using this substitution, we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}
\int\frac{\csch^2 x}{2\coth x+1}\,\mathrm{d}x
&=-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\
&=-\frac{1}{2}\ln|u|+C \\
&=-\frac{1}{2}\ln|2\coth x+1|+C.
\end{aligned}$$

The antiderivative is valid on each interval where $x\ne0$ and $2\coth x+1\ne0$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=3+\sinh x$. Differentiating gives $\mathrm{d}u=\cosh x\,\mathrm{d}x$.

When $x=0$, $u=3$. When $x=\ln 2$,

$$u=3+\frac{e^{\ln 2}-e^{-\ln 2}}{2}
=3+\frac{2-\frac{1}{2}}{2}=\frac{15}{4}.$$

Therefore,

$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{\ln 2}\frac{\cosh x}{3+\sinh x}\,\mathrm{d}x
&=\int_3^{\frac{15}{4}}\frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\
&=\left[\ln u\right]_3^{\frac{15}{4}} \\
&=\ln(\frac{15}{4})-\ln 3 \\
&=\ln\left(\frac{5}{4}\right).
\end{aligned}$$

Here $u>0$ throughout the interval, so the logarithm and substitution are defined.

knowledge_point.title: Integrating Quotients Containing Hyperbolic Functions Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=3+\sinh x$. Differentiating gives $\mathrm{d}u=\cosh x\,\mathrm{d}x$.

When $x=0$, $u=3$. When $x=\ln 10$,

$$u=3+\frac{e^{\ln 10}-e^{-\ln 10}}{2}
=3+\frac{10-\frac{1}{10}}{2}=\frac{159}{20}.$$

Therefore,

$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{\ln 10}\frac{\cosh x}{3+\sinh x}\,\mathrm{d}x
&=\int_3^{\frac{159}{20}}\frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\
&=\left[\ln u\right]_3^{\frac{159}{20}} \\
&=\ln(\frac{159}{20})-\ln 3 \\
&=\ln\left(\frac{53}{20}\right).
\end{aligned}$$

Here $u>0$ throughout the interval, so the logarithm and substitution are defined.
